html:
The Children's Crusade was a pair of popular religious marches in 1212, in France and the Rhineland, in which crowds, many of them young and poor, set out to free Jerusalem by faith and not by arms. It is a failed movement that took place in the era of the Crusades, soon after the Fourth Crusade.

In France a shepherd boy named Stephen said Christ had given him a letter for the king, and he drew crowds at Saint-Denis. In Germany, a boy called Nicholas, around Cologne, led a larger group over the Alps in summer. Many died of heat, hunger and sickness. Survivors reached Genoa in August, where the sea did not part as they hoped. Some stayed, some went on to Pisa and Rome.

At Rome, Pope Innocent III praised their zeal but released them from their vows, saying they could take the cross when they were older. Many went home on foot. The idea that children sailed from Marseille and were sold into slavery comes from later stories and is doubtful.

Most historians think "children" meant young people and the poor of all ages. The episode shows the pull of crusading among ordinary people and the Church's wary view of it. Innocent III soon called the Fourth Lateran Council to plan another crusade.
